hints: Look closely at the thickness of the wall around the large pale lumen and use the $1 \mu\text{m}$ scale bar to judge how thick it is and how wide the whole vessel is.
Think about which vessel is built only for exchange - what wall structure gives the shortest diffusion distance and allows close contact with tissue fluid?
Link the very thin wall to its cell type and the tiny lumen to the size of a red blood cell, about $7 \mu\text{m}$ across.
walkthrough:
Reading the Micrograph Like a Histologist**
You are looking at a single large space, the lumen, surrounded by an extremely thin dark line. There is no thick smooth muscle or elastic connective tissue layer outside it. Using the $1 \mu\text{m}$ bar, the whole vessel is only about $10-15 \mu\text{m}$ across. That rules out artery and vein, which are much larger and have thick walls.

Why This Must Be a Capillary**
Capillaries are the exchange vessels. Their wall is endothelium only - a single layer of flattened squamous endothelial cells. That gives a diffusion distance of about one cell, ideal for rapid exchange of oxygen, glucose, amino acids and waste between blood and tissue fluid.

Second Piece of Evidence**
The lumen is tiny, about $7 \mu\text{m}$ in diameter, just wide enough for red blood cells to squeeze through in single file. The vessel also lies directly in the tissue with no outer coats, so it is bathed in tissue fluid for exchange.
Final answer: Type: capillary. Wall is one cell thick / made of single squamous endothelial cell only; very narrow lumen approx $5-8 \mu\text{m}$; in direct contact with surrounding tissue.

hints: A semilunar valve closes when pressure on the ventricle side falls just below pressure on the artery side - find where the dashed right ventricle line crosses from above to below the solid pulmonary artery line on the falling part of the curves.
walkthrough:
When Valves Close**
The valve between right ventricle and pulmonary artery stays open while ventricular pressure is higher than arterial pressure and blood is flowing out. It snaps shut as soon as ventricular pressure drops below arterial pressure, preventing backflow.

Reading the Crossover**
On Fig. 2.2 both pressures rise together to about $3.3 \text{ kPa}$ at $0.2 \text{ s}$. Then the dashed ventricle line falls while the solid artery line stays high. They cross at about $0.24-0.25 \text{ s}$. That crossover is the moment of closure.

hints: Contraction makes pressure rise very steeply from its low resting level - find where the dashed right ventricle line first leaves its flat baseline near $0 \text{ kPa}$.
walkthrough:
Spotting Systole Starting**
When the ventricle is relaxed in diastole, its pressure is almost zero and flat. As soon as its muscle contracts, pressure shoots up almost vertically. On the dashed line that sharp upturn leaves the baseline at about $0.08-0.09 \text{ s}$.

hints: Compare the timing first - at what times do both ventricles start to rise, peak and fall back to minimum, and what does that tell you about how the heartbeat is coordinated?
Now compare the height of the peaks - think about which side of the heart must generate much more pressure and why the scale in $\text{kPa}$ would be much higher for the left side.
Link any pressure difference to where the blood is going - lungs close by versus the whole body far away - and what that means for resistance to flow.
Link the functional demand to structure - which ventricle has thicker, more muscular walls and so can exert greater force on the blood?
walkthrough:
Similarity - Same Timing**
Both ventricles beat together. The wave of excitation from the AVN passes down the bundle of His and Purkyne tissue to both ventricles at the same time, so both start to contract at about $0.08 \text{ s}$, peak at about $0.3 \text{ s}$ and relax back to minimum together. A left ventricle curve would therefore rise, peak and fall in step with the right ventricle curve in Fig. 2.2.

Difference - Much Higher Pressure on the Left**
The shape is similar but the numbers are very different. Right ventricular peak here is only about $3.3 \text{ kPa}$. The left ventricle peak systolic pressure is much higher, typically about $16 \text{ kPa}$, because it must drive blood around the entire systemic circulation.

Explaining the Difference - Destination and Resistance**
The right ventricle only pumps a short distance to the nearby lungs through the pulmonary artery, where resistance is low. The left ventricle pumps through the aorta to the whole body over a long distance against much greater resistance, so far more pressure is needed to maintain flow.

Explaining the Difference - Structure Gives Function**
To generate that extra pressure, the left ventricular wall is much thicker and more muscular than the right. More muscle means a stronger contraction and greater force exerted on the blood, producing the higher systolic pressure.

Final answer: Similarity: pressure rises and falls at same times; both ventricles contract together as excitation spreads to both simultaneously. Difference: left ventricle reaches much higher peak / systolic pressure; left ventricle pumps to whole body over greater distance against higher resistance, right ventricle only to nearby lungs; left wall is thicker and more muscular so exerts more force.
